title: Bangkok Declares Flood Disaster After 300mm of Rain Submerges Roads
summary:
Bangkok is sinking — not literally, but its streets are disappearing under water. Since Thursday, more than 300mm (12 inches) of rain has pounded the Thai capital, and on Sunday the city declared a flood disaster. All 50 districts are now emergency zones. Roads are submerged, canals have burst their banks, and traffic — already famously terrible in Bangkok — has turned into chaos.

The city's governor, Chadchart Sittipunt, said the east side was hit hardest. "The rain keeps falling and we are doing our best," he told the AFP news agency. "We are trying to pump the water out, but the water in canals are full... Every canal is now filled." He warned that the flooding is not over yet. On Sunday, Bangkok's Metropolitan Authority said the rains had subsided, but canal water levels remained high.

For people living near Bangkok's network of canals, the situation is serious. Somkid Pheuk-ngam, a 67-year-old who lives near a canal just north of central Bangkok, described the scene: "The water keeps coming in. It's hard to go out now. It's like at my waist level now. I cannot go anywhere. I have been closing my shop for two days now."

She said the flooding appears worse than in 2011, when nationwide floods hit Bangkok for three months and killed hundreds across Thailand. So far, no casualties have been reported in Bangkok from this latest disaster.

The Thai Meteorological Service forecasts more heavy rain through the week, though the low-pressure system causing the downpours is expected to move toward central Thailand. Officials have urged people to stay home and advised those near canals to move their belongings to upper floors.

Thunderstorms are common in Thailand this time of year, but extreme weather in recent days has overwhelmed Bangkok's drainage system. The city is pumping water out, but with canals already full, there's nowhere for it to go.
why_it_matters: Bangkok is a preview of a problem facing many big coastal cities: as the ground sinks, the sea rises and rainfall gets more extreme, drainage systems designed decades ago stop being enough — and the people hit first are usually those with the least money to move or rebuild.

background_read: Bangkok, Thailand's capital and largest city, is built on the flat, soft ground of the Chao Phraya River delta, and much of it sits only a metre or two above sea level.

The city is famous for its network of canals — known locally as 'klongs' — which were once main transport routes and now form part of its drainage system; when they fill up, there is nowhere left for rainwater to go.
Because the ground is soft and groundwater has been pumped out for decades, parts of Bangkok have been slowly sinking, while sea levels rise at the same time — a double squeeze for a low-lying city.

Thailand's monsoon season brings heavy rain every year, and the Thai Meteorological Service (the government agency that tracks weather and issues forecasts) is the body now warning of more rain, with the low-pressure system expected to drift toward central Thailand.

The 2011 floods that a resident compares today's disaster to were among the worst in Thailand's modern history, with monsoon rains and dam releases inundating large parts of the country, including Bangkok, for months.

Chadchart Sittipunt, Bangkok's elected governor (the city's top official, chosen by voters rather than appointed nationally), has made flood management and drainage one of his signature issues — but no city government can pump water out faster than a stalled storm pours it in.

perspectives.description: No casualties have been reported in Bangkok, and the governor's team has been pumping water and issuing clear advice to stay home — a sign that early warnings and emergency zones can save lives even when the water wins.

Canals are already full, roads are submerged and small shop owners like Somkid Pheuk-ngam are losing days of income, which raises hard questions about whether Bangkok's drainage system can cope with the heavier rain it now faces.

perspectives.perspective: Geography and history explain the risk
perspectives.description: The city sits on soft river-delta ground that is slowly sinking, and Thailand has flooded badly before — notably in 2011, when waters covered much of the country for months — so this is a recurring pattern rather than a one-off freak event.

perspectives.perspective: What the city should do next
perspectives.description: Longer term, Bangkok may need bigger pumps, more water-storage areas and stricter building rules, but with the low-pressure system moving toward central Thailand, the immediate question is whether other provinces are ready for the same deluge.
